title: Exam Anxiety Affects Over One-Third of Surveyed Nepalese Medical Students - Bioengineer.org
description: Exam Anxiety Affects Over One-Third of Surveyed Nepalese Medical Students  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
A descriptive cross-sectional investigation conducted among undergraduate medical students in Kathmandu, Nepal, found that 36.2 percent of participants experienced high exam anxiety, spanning levels classified as moderately high to extremely high. Published in BMC Medical Education, the study sought to determine the prevalence of exam anxiety and evaluate its potential associations with academic and study-related factors within a local educational setting. According to the research team, exam anxiety constitutes a significant psychological concern among medical students globally, yet empirical evidence and epidemiological data from Nepal have remained limited. Within this specific cohort of future physicians, more than one-third met the criteria for high exam anxiety, demonstrating that testing-related psychological distress was prevalent among the surveyed undergraduates.

The findings revealed distinct demographic patterns in how exam anxiety manifested across the student cohort. In particular, female students reported significantly higher levels of exam anxiety than their male peers, a disparity that was confirmed through statistical analysis (p = 0.002). In addition to gender-based differences, exam anxiety was closely linked to objective measures of academic performance. Students experiencing high exam anxiety were significantly more likely to have failed their most recent major examination compared to classmates who reported normal anxiety levels (p < 0.001). The investigators noted that this marked correlation highlighted an association between elevated test anxiety and poorer recent academic standing within the institution.

Habits related to daily academic preparation and coursework routines were also significantly associated with the presence of exam anxiety. When examining self-reported study behaviors, the researchers observed that students with high exam anxiety dedicated fewer total study hours to their work than those categorized with normal anxiety levels, a difference that reached statistical significance (p = 0.031). Furthermore, preparation strategies before test days differed substantially between the two groups; students suffering from high exam anxiety were significantly less likely to revise their academic material prior to examinations compared to peers with normal anxiety levels (p < 0.001). Together, both shorter study durations and an absence of pre-exam revision characterized the higher-anxiety student group.

To assess these conditions, the research team conducted a descriptive cross-sectional study among 384 undergraduate medical students enrolled at the Nepalese Army Institute of Health Sciences in Kathmandu, Nepal. The investigators utilized a proportionate stratified random sampling strategy to assemble the study cohort from the student body. Data collection was performed using a self-administered questionnaire designed to record sociodemographic characteristics alongside standardized mental health measurements. To evaluate anxiety, the study administered the Westside Test Anxiety Scale, which classified participant exam anxiety levels across a structured continuum extending from comfortably low to extremely high.

For analytical evaluation, the authors employed chi-square tests and independent t-tests to evaluate the statistical significance of differences and associations across participant groups. The researchers concluded that exam anxiety was present at moderately high to extremely high levels in more than one-third of the undergraduate medical students in this Nepalese cohort. Overall, the analysis demonstrated that high exam anxiety was significantly associated with female gender, failure in the last major examination, fewer reported study hours, and a lack of revision before exams. The authors emphasized that these findings provide critical baseline insight into how academic distress and study-related behaviors intersect among medical students in Nepal.

title: Young trekker found dead after going missing near Nepal's Badimalika temple - The Star
description: Young trekker found dead after going missing near Nepal's Badimalika temple  The Star
publisher.title: The Star
full_article:
BAJURA; A 20-year-old man who went missing while visiting the Badimalika religious site in Bajura, Nepal, has been found dead.

Manish Bohara, a resident of Daiji in Bedkot Municipality, Kanchanpur, had gone missing while visiting the pilgrimage site. Bajura Chief District Officer Muktiram Rijal confirmed to Kantipur that Bohara's body was found near Triveni Patan in Badimalika.

A security team was deployed by helicopter from the district headquarters on Sunday morning to search for him. Rijal said continuous bad weather, snowfall and freezing temperatures may have caused his death.

A search team from the Ishwaribaks Battalion, based in Martadi, found Bohara's body near Triveni Patan, Rijal said. Authorities are making arrangements to airlift the body and the security personnel involved in the search, he added.

Meanwhile, another trekker, 21-year-old Sagar Karki of Krishnapur Municipality-2 in Kanchanpur, was rescued by helicopter on Saturday afternoon after being stranded at Triveni Patan following heavy snowfall. He was flown to Martadi.

Karki had been staying at a shelter in Triveni Patan since Friday after snowfall blocked his return route from the Badimalika temple, located at an altitude of 4,200 metres.

A group of five people had set out for Badimalika from the district headquarters, Martadi, on October 26. The group included Bohara and Karki from Sudurpaschim and three others from eastern Nepal. The three trekkers from eastern Nepal had already returned. - Kathmandu Post/ANN

Kathmandu, November 9

A total of 175 foreign nationals were deported from Nepal during the months of Shrawan, Bhadra and Ashoj.

The government has not provided details about the reasons for their deportation.

According to the Ministry of Home Affairs’ quarterly progress report for the past three months, 52 foreign nationals were deported in Shrawan, 59 in Bhadra and 64 in Ashoj.

The figures have been included under the work carried out by the ministry’s Border and Immigration Section.

All government offices are required to publish quarterly progress reports. Under Section 5(3) of the Right to Information Act, 2007, and Rule 3 of the Right to Information Regulations, 2008, public bodies must proactively disclose updated information at least once every three months.

Section 5(3) of the Act states that public bodies must update and publish such information at least every three months, taking into account the time of their establishment and development.

The Ministry of Home Affairs has also published its latest quarterly progress report in line with the law’s objective of making the activities of public bodies transparent, accountable and open to the public.

title: Nepal: Education unions turn Go Public! campaign training into local action - Education International
description: Nepal: Education unions turn Go Public! campaign training into local action  Education International
publisher.title: Education International
full_article:
Thirty unionists from four Education International (EI) member organisations have developed practical campaigns to win greater investment in public education, strengthen union organisation, and mobilise communities across Nepal.

Organised by EI in cooperation with the Danish Union of Teachers (Danmarks Lærerforening, DLF), the workshop focused on building the campaigning power of EI member organisations. Participants identified barriers to quality public education and prepared initiatives on school funding, dropout prevention, school meals, safe drinking water, and digital learning. They also turned the demands of Education International’s Go Public! Fund Education campaign into concrete local organising plans.

The workshop held in the capital city Kathmandu from October 30th to November 1st, 2026, brought together equal numbers of women and men from the Nepal Teachers’ Association (NTA), Nepal National Teachers’ Association (NNTA), Institutional Schools’ Teachers’ Union (ISTU), and Nepal School Employees’ Council (NSEC).

From regional commitments to local campaigns

The workshop followed the 10th EI Asia-Pacific Regional Conference, held in Jakarta, Indonesia, in October 2026, where education unions reaffirmed the need for sustained public investment, decent working conditions, and strong, inclusive public education systems.

“Across Asia-Pacific, education unions are campaigning for greater public investment, better working conditions, and stronger public education. The campaigns developed here show how unions can turn regional commitments into local action, build public support, and influence education policies,” said Anand Singh, EI Asia-Pacific Regional Director.

Campaigning and organising workers and communities

Participants stressed that securing increased education funding requires organising members, building alliances with parents and communities, and taking credible proposals to local authorities. In the meantime, these campaign activities strengthen and empower unions.

“Demanding more education funding is not enough. We must organise our members, engage communities, and approach local governments with achievable proposals. Campaigning can make our branches stronger and build public trust,” said Hansa Bahadur Shahi of NNTA.

For Tarachandra of NTA, “safe drinking water is a basic need for our students. By working with parents, communities, and local government to address this problem, we can improve our school, bring union members together, and earn public trust.”

“Quality public education requires adequate funding and proper support for everyone working in schools. Our campaign seeks free education for children and better conditions for school employees. Working with parents and communities will also strengthen our organisation,” also noted NSEC’s Bibika Malla.

Defending rights across the education sector

The workshop also highlighted the insecure working conditions faced by teachers in Nepal’s private schools and the importance of linking the Go Public! Fund Education campaign with the defence of labour rights throughout the education sector.

“Many private school teachers still lack job security, fair salaries, and social protection. Our campaigns must bring teachers, parents, and communities together to secure employment contracts, decent working conditions, and fundamental labour rights,” acknowledged Hom Kumar Thapa of ISTU.

Participants also committed to advancing their plans through their union branches. NTA, NNTA, ISTU, and NSEC will support follow-up action to organise members, engage communities, and drive Go Public! forward at local level.

Anand Singh, EI consultant Sagar Nath, and union leaders facilitated the sessions. Dong Tolentino of Building and Wood Workers’ International addressed the opening session, underscoring the wider trade union movement’s stake in defending quality public services and workers’ rights.

International trade union movement stands with Nepal’s unions

Meeting in Kathmandu for their Annual Coordination Meeting, representatives of the International Trade Union Confederation Asia-Pacific, Global Union Federations, and Trade Union Solidarity Support Organisations further expressed strong solidarity with Nepal’s trade union movement at a “critical moment”.

The organisations voiced serious concern over measures taken by the Government of Nepal that undermine trade union rights, particularly in public services. They stressed that “administrative reforms, political neutrality, and the pursuit of administrative efficiency must not be used to justify weakening independent trade unions, restricting workers’ fundamental rights, or undermining established mechanisms of social dialogue.”

They reaffirmed that freedom of association and the rights to organise and bargain collectively are fundamental, internationally recognised rights. Nepal’s Constitution guarantees workers the right to form and join trade unions and to engage in collective bargaining, while the country’s ratification of International Labour Organization’s Convention No. 98 commits the government to uphold these rights.

Their joint statement calls on the Government of Nepal to reverse measures that undermine freedom of association and collective bargaining, fully respect constitutional guarantees and international labour standards, ensure that public sector workers can organise without interference or discrimination, and engage in genuine social dialogue with representative unions. It also calls for the immediate restoration of workers’ representation in tripartite bodies, Education Councils and the Education Board, the Social Security Fund, the Foreign Employment Board, and the Central Labour Advisory Councils.

The International Trade Union Confederation Asia-Pacific, Global Union Federations, and Trade Union Solidarity Support Organisations also encouraged Nepal’s unions “to strengthen their unity, solidarity, and cooperation in defending workers’ rights, protecting independent trade unionism, and advancing social justice.”

They went on reaffirming their readiness to support affiliated organisations and the wider trade union movement in protecting fundamental rights, upholding international labour standards, and strengthening democratic trade unionism in Nepal.

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle left for Türkiye on Monday to attend the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), where Nepal is expected to push for stronger international support on climate finance, adaptation and the growing impacts of climate change on vulnerable mountain countries.

Wagle flew to Antalya, the host city of the climate summit, aboard a Turkish Airlines flight from Tribhuvan International Airport.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal is leading the Nepali delegation at the summit and has already arrived in Antalya. Khanal is scheduled to take part in high-level discussions and represent Nepal in international climate negotiations.

title: Human-crow relations show strain as Kathmandu observes annual day of the crow - news - Mongabay
description: Human-crow relations show strain as Kathmandu observes annual day of the crow  news - Mongabay
publisher.title: news - Mongabay
full_article:
In Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, house crows are venerated as messengers of god and ecologists praise their role as nature’s scavengers, but people are increasingly wary about their presence.

A Valley-wide study found crows to be the most common species at urban sites and while no published trend shows their numbers rising, anecdotal evidence suggests a positive trend.

Urban sprawl, fewer old trees and plentiful food waste favor generalist birds, like house crows and black kites, which now nest on power lines and poles.

After an avian influenza outbreak at the city’s Central Zoo involving crows, a Department of Livestock Services veterinary officer has called for closer surveillance of the birds, but ecologists say poor waste management and habitat loss are the real problems. See All Key Ideas

KATHMANDU — Ramesh Dulal was 13 years old when he began “communicating” with crows. He started making sounds resembling the crows, who would respond by gathering around him, he recalls.

Popularly known as kagé , crows are called kaag in Nepali, and Nepal observes an annual day of the crow, called Kaag Tihar , which falls around the Hindu festival of Deepawali, or Diwali. On this day, Dulal, now 35, organizes what he calls the Crow Conference every year. This year, it was on Saturday last week, Nov. 7.

At the event every year, Dulal, a folk music singer and activist, holds a microphone and produces a series of guttural calls, “caw … caw … caw,” imitating a crow. As his calls echo through powerful speakers, flocks of crows gather from surrounding trees, rooftops and electrical poles. After several minutes, he stops and addresses the people who have come to witness the event. He speaks about the religious significance of crows and their ecological role.

Then the conference ends.

While Dulal wholeheartedly welcomes crows to his event, many residents in Kathmandu would rather shoo them away, especially after the birds were blamed for a bird flu outbreak at the Central Zoo. But crows are thriving in the city as trees disappear and waste piles up, and birds that live on scraps are gaining ground over those that need trees.

A house crow looks on during the morning prayers at the Buddhist Bodha Stupa, Bodha, Kathmandu. Image by Wonderlane via Flickr (CC BY-NC 2.0).

The messengers of a god

Regardless of their reputation within the community, the birds have long been a part of Kathmandu’s cultural life. Devotees have dedicated a temple to the bird in the eastern fringe of the Kathmandu Valley. Similarly on the first day of the five-day-long festival of lights, Hindus worship crows as messengers of Yama, the god of death. People offer them garlands and food to seek their blessings for a long life.

Beyond religion, crows play an important ecological function: They help remove decaying waste. “Crows help keep the surroundings clean by feeding on carcasses.,” says Kamal Raj Gosai, an ornithologist and associate professor at Tri-Chandra Multiple Campus, Tribhuvan University, Nepal. “They are often regarded as nature’s scavengers,”

Crows are also considered highly intelligent and adaptable, and studies have shown they can adjust to a wide range of environments, including densely populated cities.

A crow eats food offered for crows on Kaag Tihar in Kathmandu. Image by Poonamkulung via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Urban expansion and a changing bird community

Despite their cultural and ecological importance, crows’ relations with humans are strained for no fault of their own, researchers say. Citing changes in the city’s habitat and waste management practices, which favor their population growth, they say humans are the reason crows are falling into disrepute.

A study based on three decades of satellite imagery found that Kathmandu’s urban area expanded by approximately 124% between 1989 and 2018. Another study found that green space in Kathmandu Metropolitan City declined by 54% between 1975 and 2025. Experts say these changes are directly affecting urban biodiversity.

According to ornithologists, the Kathmandu Valley’s bird community is becoming ecologically lopsided. Native species that depend on specific habitats are being displaced, while generalists, which can survive on varied food in varied environments, are becoming more common. House crows ( Corvus splendens ) and black kites ( Milvus migrans ) are among the species that have become conspicuous in the urban landscape.

Bird Conservation Nepal has counted birds along 24 fixed transects across the valley every year since 2016 . House crows regularly rank among the most commonly recorded species, placing among the top five in its winter 2022 count. A valley-wide study led by Dinesh Bhusal of Nepal’s Tribhuvan University, published in 2024, found the house crow was the most common species at urban sites, and suggests that degrading green space may help such generalist species colonize the city.

As roads were widened and the city grew, the road department removed many old trees. With fewer natural perches and nesting sites, crows have increasingly turned to electrical wires and utility poles, the Bhusal-led study suggests.

Ornithologist Gosai says the removal of old trees during road expansion, particularly along the Kathmandu Ring Road, a 27-kilometer (16-mile) eight-lane highway, has reduced habitat for several species, including egrets and crows. Meanwhile, abundant food waste has allowed crows and black kites to stay concentrated in the heart of the city.

“Large quantities of discarded food and exposed waste from meat shops have contributed to the unusual increase in crows and kites in Kathmandu,” he tells Mongabay. “Crows are intelligent birds. Even when trees are unavailable, they can quickly find alternative nesting sites in telephone towers and crevices in new buildings.”

Amid rapid infrastructure expansion and the loss of mature urban trees, house crows make use of remaining boughs to nest above a crowded Kathmandu neighborhood. Image courtesy Dinesh Bhusal.

Black kites and a house crow at Bagmati River in Bagmati Province, Nepal. Image by Sudan Shrestha via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

When urban greening favors only a few species

The kinds of trees planted in cities can also influence which birds survive. Hem Bahadur Katuwal, a bird ecologist from Nepal at the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in Yunnan, southwest China, says removing mature urban trees displaces specialist birds, which depend on particular habitats.

“When old and large trees are cut down, specialist birds lose their habitats. Eventually, only functional generalist species, such as crows, which can survive under almost any conditions, remain,” he tells Mongabay.

Some greening policies may unintentionally favor adaptable species. Under local building regulations, homeowners are generally required to plant trees when obtaining approval for house construction, and many choose avocado, partly because it is easy to grow. The Bhusal study found that crows, the most abundant nesting birds in the valley, nested in non-native trees such as avocado, as well as on electricity lines and poles. But Katuwal cautions that more tree cover does not automatically mean more biodiversity. “Planting only one species of tree cannot protect bird diversity,” he says. “Instead, it [could] encourage monoculture.”

Gosai disagrees on the role of avocados. He says that planting avocado or other trees in private compounds does not necessarily benefit crows in a meaningful way or restore ecological balance, because crows nest in a variety of structures, from telephone towers to buildings, whether or not traditional trees are available. He links their growing presence around rivers and other urban areas to food in garbage dumps.

Open dumping of waste along riverbanks and in public spaces, a common practice in Nepal, gives crows easy access to food in large numbers. Image by Wolf Gordon Clifton / Animal People, Inc. via Flickr (CC BY-NC 2.0).

Nuisance and questions about disease

For many Kathmandu residents, the growing presence of crows is a nuisance. Droppings, food scraps and occasional pieces of meat can foul rooftops, water tanks and living spaces.

Mamta Shah, a resident of Bhaktapur, a city in eastern Kathmandu Valley, says she has struggled since crows began nesting around her house. “I am fed up with crows coming and staying around my house,” she says. “What is the point of them sitting here when they leave pieces of meat and all kinds of waste around the house?” She worries that crows carry pathogens along with the remains they bring from elsewhere.

Crows have also been linked to avian influenza. A few months ago, an outbreak of bird flu at Nepal’s Central Zoo, the city’s only zoo, involved crows. The highly pathogenic H5N1 virus is believed to have entered animal enclosures through wild crows moving freely around the city. More than 60 animals and birds, including rare species, died. Others were culled to prevent further spread.

Unique ecological niche

Veterinarians say the outbreak fits a wider pattern. Krishna Prasad Acharya, a veterinarian based in Kathmandu, says that the crow occupies an “unusual ecological niche” as it can find a way, with ease, through human settlements, garbage sites, poultry farms as well as natural areas. This is a risk in the context of Kathmandu: With no land use planning, human populations, poultry farms and wetlands lie close together, heightening the risk of cross-species transmission of diseases.

Ecologists caution against treating crows as the problem. “Any species can become infected with a disease,” Katuwal tells Mongabay. “The idea of eliminating crows from cities or treating them as enemies is entirely misguided. Crows perform an important service by helping clean up urban waste and carcasses. The problem is not the crows; it is our poor waste management and the destruction of habitats. We need to change our negative perception of these birds.”

Gosai also stresses the need to expand green spaces and plant a diversity of species. He says he believes that planting suitable new trees could draw birds away from residential structures and towards more appropriate habitats, even though many old trees were lost along the Kathmandu Ring Road.

Open dumping of waste along riverbanks and in public spaces, a common practice in Nepal, gives crows easy access to food in large numbers, and experts say that same proximity to unmanaged waste can raise the risk of pathogen transmission.

Household debris and plastic waste line the inundated banks of the Hanumantey River in Kaushaltar, Bhakatpur in Kathmandu Valley. While rapid habitat alteration displaces sensitive river species, opportunistic urban scavengers like crows thrive on the open refuse left behind by unchecked municipal expansion. Image by Gobinda Pokharel/Mongabay.

Can Kathmandu make space for its birds?

Local administration Kathmandu Metropolitan City says it has begun addressing bird conservation and green-space protection. Acting Mayor Sunita Dangol says bird conservation has been incorporated into several aspects of its environmental policy this year. “We have included bird conservation in different aspects of our environmental policy this year,” she tells Mongabay.

After concerns were raised about decorative wires and lights installed around trees in the name of beautification, the municipal executive board decided to remove them. Dangol says the city is prioritizing protection of existing trees over felling them for road expansion. “We have adopted a policy of reconsidering road designs to protect trees during expansion projects,” she says. “We are also developing clear guidelines for urban tree planting in consultation with botanists.”

Dulal, who organizes the crow conference, says his relationship with crows goes beyond mimicry. His annual event is an attempt to change how people see birds that are increasingly unwelcome in the city to which they have adapted. “People have started believing that crows directly spread diseases,” he says. “But these birds actually contribute enormously to keeping the environment clean.”

Craning your neck to see the peaks of impossibly high Himalayan mountains feels like a moment of pure disbelief. It doesn't matter if you've been to every other mountain range on Earth; if you haven't been to Nepal, then you surely won't believe just how high mountains can be. However, they're not only high. They are magnificent in shape and length, and the spirituality connected to them is an enlightening experience for many. Everest may be the granddaddy, but Nepal is home to many other mountains that could easily be considered wonders of the world.

Nepal boasts eight of the ten highest mountains on the planet, and there are treks throughout the country that allow you to get the best possible views of them all. Some of them are short day trips, while others are multi-week adventures. There are trails for all levels of fitness and experience, but hiking this network isn't for everyone. Facilities are minimal, and accommodation is mostly rustic, with teahouses offering unheated rooms and blankets that have often seen better days.

That said, hearty meals are shared around wood stoves, fostering a communal feel, and the Nepalese hospitality is something that lingers long after the memories of snow-capped peaks begin to fade. With a little research, you can easily have the time of your life enjoying the splendor of the Himalayas while feeling proud that you were able to give up some of your creature comforts. At least for a short time anyway. Through personal experience, traveler tales, and online reviews, we have compiled some of the best and most popular treks to experience while on a trip to Nepal.

description: Nepal Airlines’ Rs 34 billion loan for four aircraft rises to Rs 55.92 billion  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, November 9

The outstanding loan taken by Nepal Airlines Corporation (NAC) to purchase four aircraft has increased from Rs 34 billion to Rs 55.92 billion.

The corporation had borrowed the money from the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) and the Citizens Investment Trust (CIT), with the government standing as guarantor, to purchase two wide-body and two narrow-body aircraft.

According to data from the Financial Comptroller General Office, the initial principal amount guaranteed for the aircraft purchases was Rs 34 billion. The outstanding liability has now reached Rs 55.92 billion.

The EPF provided Rs 12 billion for the purchase of the wide-body aircraft, while the CIT extended another Rs 12 billion for the same purpose. Earlier, the EPF had also lent Rs 10 billion to NAC to purchase narrow-body aircraft.

By the end of the last fiscal year 2025/26, the outstanding principal had increased to Rs 44.68 billion, while the accumulated interest stood at Rs 11.24 billion.

This brings the corporation’s total outstanding debt for the four aircraft to Rs 55.92 billion.

title: Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026 to Showcase Projects Worth $17 Billion - Ratopati
description: Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026 to Showcase Projects Worth $17 Billion  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The government is set to 'showcase' strategic and mega projects worth approximately 17 billion US dollars (26.5 trillion rupees) among international investors at the 'Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026' to be held on December 9 and 10.

Large projects in 9 sectors including roads, energy, urban development, industry, and technology (AI data center) are being presented with the goal of making the country a 100 billion dollar economy within the next 5 to 7 years.

The government has also stated that it has reached the final stage of preparing to amend 494 clauses of 59 laws before the summit to attract foreign investment and ensure investor security. At a program organized in the capital on Thursday, on the eve of the Infrastructure Summit, information was given that 23 projects worth 17 billion US dollars proposed by various ministries, departments, and government-owned companies have already been listed.

Similarly, projects to be presented by the private sector have not yet been listed. This summit is being organized primarily by the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development and the Confederation of Nepalese Industries (CNI), with co-organization by the Investment Board Nepal, the Federation of Contractors' Associations of Nepal (FCAN), and the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI).

The summit will present a total of 23 projects to investors with investment models, including 6 road transport sector projects, 5 energy projects, 4 urban development projects, 3 industry projects, and 1 each in agriculture, multipurpose, tourism, tech infrastructure, and mixed (tunnel and city) projects.

Tunnels/Expressways and Urbanization

Giving high priority to transport infrastructure, the summit includes 6 road projects and a mixed-city project with tunnels under the Ministry of Infrastructure for showcase. These include the much-anticipated Kohalpur-Surkhet Expressway for high-speed travel and the Butwal-Pokhara Expressway, considered a tourist and trade lifeline.

Similarly, to reduce geographical difficulties and traffic congestion, the Daunne tunnel on the Butwal-Narayangadh section of the East-West Highway, the Dharan-Leuti tunnel as a lifeline for the Koshi Province, and the Majhitar-Shaktikhor tunnel connecting Bagmati and Gandaki, along with a mixed-city project, are being presented.

Nicholas Pandey, Chairman of the Federation of Nepalese Contractors' Associations, stated that the traditional method of measuring infrastructure development needs to change, and these projects will reduce travel time. Pandey said, 'Infrastructure is not just measured by how many kilometers of road are blacktopped annually. These tunnels and expressways are essential for reaching Chitwan/Pokhara from Kathmandu in 3 hours, Kakarbhitta in 6 hours, Kanchanpur in 9 hours, and Mechi-Mahakali in 12 hours.'

Similarly, the Kathmandu Valley Development Authority and the Ministry of Urban Development have listed 4 urban infrastructure projects for planned and modern urbanization.

Energy and Transmission Line: 5 Major Hydropower and Transmission Projects

Five major energy projects will be presented to investors at the summit, led by the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation and government companies. These include the 1061 MW Upper Arun Hydropower Project, the 635 MW Dudhkoshi Reservoir Project, the much-anticipated Tamor Reservoir Project, and the 1200 MW Budhi Gandaki Hydropower Project being advanced through the Budhi Gandaki Hydropower Company.

In addition, the strategically important Karnali and Bheri HVDC transmission line for transmitting the generated electricity to the national grid and for cross-border trade will also be showcased. Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle, recalling the success of private investment in the energy sector, claimed that the private sector is now open to transmission and trade as well. 'We started with 262 MW in the Panchayat era, and today our electricity generation has reached 2700 MW, with the private sector contributing 75 to 80 percent,' Finance Minister Wagle said. 'Now, the government is amending laws to provide open access to transmission lines, allowing the private sector to trade electricity domestically and internationally.'

Industry, Mines, and Agriculture: From Naubasta to Urbanization of the Valley

Under the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, the Industrial Area Management Limited will bring three major projects to the summit: the Naubasta Industrial Area in Banke, the Shaktikhor Industrial Area in Chitwan, and the Dhaubadi Iron Ore Mine in Nawalparasi, with the goal of becoming self-reliant by producing domestic iron.

Similarly, in the agriculture sector, the Mustang Apple Farming and Commercial Processing Center, which supports the high-mountain economy, has been included as an agricultural project.

Tech Infrastructure and Tourism: From AI Data Center to Nijgadh Airport

Keeping in mind the digital economy and future technology, the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology has proposed two strategic projects. A project to establish a state-of-the-art 'AI Data Center' in Rolwaling or Mustang, utilizing Nepal's cold climate and green energy, will be showcased. Additionally, the 'Multi-hub ICT Park, Kathmandu' project is being presented to investors for the integrated development of the information technology industry in the capital.

The Ministry of Tourism and Civil Aviation has included the Nijgadh International Airport, considered a milestone in the country's air connectivity, for development under a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model. The Khaptad Integrated Eco-Tourism Project for the tourism development of the Far-Western region has also been listed as a major attraction of the summit.

Exhibition of Investment-Friendly Laws Along with Projects: Ministers' Commitment

To address the problem of project announcements in the past not moving forward due to legal hurdles, the government has this time put forward proposals to amend 494 clauses of 59 laws.

Minister for Physical Infrastructure and Transport, Sunil Lamshal, clarified that this year's summit is focused on breaking the old pattern of just showing numbers. Lamshal said, 'Investors will not come just by pitching projects worth so many billion dollars as in the past. Investors need security of investment, protection of labor, market guarantees, and an environment where investment does not fail. Therefore, showcasing the laws that we have amended to ensure all these is the main objective of this summit.'

Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Sobita Gautam, stated that the work of amending 494 clauses of 59 laws has reached the final stage before the summit. Minister Gautam said, 'Although the parliament is not in session, if necessary, the government will bring the laws before the summit through an ordinance. Even during festivals like Tihar and Chhath, the bureaucracy has been working behind closed doors without taking leave.'

According to Sudeep Dhakal, Policy and Good Governance Advisor to the Prime Minister, the proposed laws specify legal timeframes for 190 administrative processes. It has made mandatory provisions for obtaining industrial establishment permits within 15 days, land ceiling exemption and compensation determination within 60 days, tree felling within 30 days, and PPA finalization within 90 days. Dhakal claims that the implementation of all these 23 projects will be ensured thereafter.

Stakeholders from the private sector, however, have emphasized the need to boost the morale of domestic investors to attract foreign investment. Anjan Shrestha, President of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, stressed the need to first boost the morale of domestic investors to attract foreign capital for large projects. Birendra Raj Pandey, President of the Confederation of Nepalese Industries, informed that the main theme of this year's summit is 'Building for a Resilient Future,' and projects have been selected based on physical, economic, and institutional resilience.

International Roadshows Being Held

To attract international financial institutions and multinational companies to these projects, the government is organizing 'roadshows' in four major cities. After the preliminary session held at Hotel Soaltee in Kathmandu, special roadshows are scheduled to be held in New Delhi, India on November 19, Dubai, UAE on November 25, and Beijing, China on November 30.

In line with the government's policy of 'Big Hit in Good Governance, Big Bang in Economic Reform, and Big Push in Infrastructure,' it is believed that if foreign direct and domestic private investment can be attracted to these 23 projects, the roadmap to make Nepal a 100 billion dollar economy within the next five years will take concrete shape.

Kathmandu. Ravi Bopara of Chitwan Rhinos has completed his seventh half-century in the Nepal Premier League (NPL).

While chasing a target of 181 runs against Kathmandu Gurkhas, Bopara scored 55 runs off 35 balls before getting out. He hit 2 fours and 3 sixes.

Chitwan has scored 164 runs for the loss of 7 wickets in 19.2 overs. Now, Chitwan needs 17 runs in 4 balls to win.

Earlier, Kamil Mishra scored 28 and Arjun Saud scored 23 for Chitwan. Sahana Arachchige took 2 wickets, while Ganesh Gautam, Karan KC, Santosh Yadav, and Jahandad Khan took 1 wicket each for Kathmandu.

Kathmandu had scored 180 runs for the loss of 8 wickets in the stipulated 20 overs.
